paper_title: Benchmarking Obstacle-Conditioned Safety in Household Robot Navigation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Safe household navigation requires robots to regulate clearance and speed according to what an obstacle is and how close it is, without unnecessary conservatism. Yet existing evaluations do not test whether semantic safety distinctions are reflected in continuous motion. To that end, we introduce OSMA-Bench, an Obstacle-Conditioned Safe Motion Adaptation Benchmark built on spatially matched scenario sets that differ only in obstacle type. We also propose the \emph{Semantic Sensitivity Index} (SSI), which measures whether clearance and distance-dependent speed and smoothness follow the caution ordering of obstacles. Evaluating VLM-based and vision-language-action (VLA) policies on the benchmark, we find that neither consistently adapts its motion to obstacle safety, even with explicit safety prompts. Our analysis shows that the policies can correctly distinguish obstacles by safety relevance but fail to reflect this distinction in the motion parameters or actions they produce. For VLM-based policies, which recognize the obstacle and then generate a navigation program, adding an explicit parameter-inference step between these two stages improves adaptation. These findings expose a gap in \emph{semantic-to-motion grounding}, highlighting the need to translate semantic caution into appropriately safe motion.

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: Safe household navigation requires robots to regulate clearance and speed according to what an obstacle is and how close it is, without unnecessary conservatism. Yet existing evaluations do not test whether semantic safety distinctions are reflected in continuous motion. To that end, we introduce OSMA-Bench, an Obstacle-Conditioned Safe Motion Adaptation Benchmark built on spatially matched scenario sets that differ only in obstacle type. sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: As robots are moving from industrial settings into homes, they must navigate around people, pets, and objects with different safety implications (Wachsmuth et al., 2015; Zachiotis et al., 2018; Szot et al., 2021; Yenamandra et al., 2023; Soni et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025c; ISO, 2014). Safe navigation around such entities requires obstacle-conditioned safe motion adaptation, which goes beyond collision avoidance: robot must adapt its motion to each obstacles safety implications and to how closely its route passes it. As illustrated in Figure 1, even when both paths are collision-free, robot should keep more clearance and move more slowly past child than past trash bin, and slow down further as it gets closer. This caution must also be selective, since uniform conservatism toward every obstacle would needlessly sacrifice efficiency. Achieving this requires semantic-to-motion grounding: policy must infer an appropriate level of caution from an obstacles semantics and translate it into clearance, proximity-dependent speed, and executed motion. Foundation models are natural candidates: VLMs can interpret safety-relevant semantics to inform motion planning, and VLAs generate actions directly from visual observations and language instructions. Although both are widely used in robotic systems (Huang et al., 2023; Nasiriany et al., 2024b; NVIDIA et al., 2025b; NVIDIA, 2025; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025), it remains unclear whether their executed trajectories exhibit this capability. Existing evaluations do not answer this question. Human-aware and social-navigation benchmarks (Li et al., 2024; Dong et al., 2026; Biswas et al., 2022; Fang et al., 2026) measure executed motion but focus on navigation around people, not on whether motion is calibrated to the safety implications of diverse obstacles. Embodied-safety evaluations for foundation models (Zhang et al., 2025b; Sermanet et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2025) instead assess task completion, constraint compliance, or refusal of hazardous instructions, not whether semantic

Evaluating semantic-to-motion grounding requires two components: spatially matched comparisons that isolate obstacle identity from route geometry, and metric that tests whether motion follows the expected ordering of caution across obstacles. We introduce OSMA-Bench, an Obstacle-Conditioned Safe Motion Adaptation Benchmark that provides both. Its matched comparisons vary only the obstacle type while fixing the obstacle position, surrounding layout and route, and are repeated across diverse layouts and routes. The obstacles span three caution tiersLiving, Fragile, and Robust, in descending order of expected caution motivated by ISO risk assessment principles (ISO, 2010) and social navigation research (Althoff et al., 2012; Marvel & Norcross, 2017; Moller et al., 2021; Singamaneni et al., 2024). We also introduce the Semantic Sensitivity Index (SSI), diagnostic metric that tests whether clearance, together with speed and smoothness as function of distance to the obstacle, follows this ordering. Together, OSMA-Bench assess whether policy adapts its motion to an obstacles safety implications, beyond merely reaching the goal without collision. Using OSMA-Bench, we find that VLMand VLA-based policies do not consistently exhibits this adaptation, even with explicit safety prompting. Our analysis on VLM shows that safety-relevant distinctions are accessible during isolated motionparameter inference but weaken when task-execution code and motion parameters are jointly generated; separating the two improves motion adaptation. For VLAs, prompting and action-selection interventions provide only limited recovery, highlighting insufficient semantic-to-motion grounding across both policy families. In summary, our contributions are threefold: (1) We introduce OSMA-Bench, simulation benchmark that evaluates obstacle-conditioned safe motion adaptation through matched comparisons: each comparison varies only the obstacle while holding spatial conditions fixed, and is repeated across diverse layouts and routes. (2) We propose Semantic Sensitivity Index (SSI) which quantifies the extent to which differences in executed motion across obstacle follow the expected caution ordering. (3) We identify insufficient semantic-to-motion grounding in the evaluated VLMand VLA-based policies: safety-relevant knowledge is available but does not reliably guide executed motion, highlighting the need to improve how semantic safety judgments inform motion decisions.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORKS
sections.content: Safety Evaluation in Embodied Robotics. Existing evaluations examine both navigation behavior and the safety of task decisions and execution. Social-navigation frameworks evaluate executed trajectories around people (Tsoi et al., 2020; Biswas et al., 2022), while human-aware navigation consider dynamic human interactions and socially appropriate path selection (Li et al., 2024; Dong et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2026). Complementary evaluations assess navigation-relevant visual reasoning: NaviTrace evaluates image-space navigation traces, SocialNav-SUB examines social scene understanding, and MovSafeBench tests judgments of potentially hazardous scenarios (Windecker et al., 2026; Munje et al., 2025; Taniguchi et al., 2026). Existing embodied-safety evaluation focus on task decisions and actions satisfy safety requirements. ASIMOV and SAFEMIND assess safety-

BadRobot and ANNIE further examine adversarial robustness to harmful instructions and sensory perturbations, respectively (Zhang et al., 2025b; Huang et al., 2025). However, each evaluation paradigm captures only part of the problem: socialand human-aware navigation benchmarks focus primarily on interactions with people, embodied-safety evaluations assess safety judgments rather than executed motion, and neither provides paired comparisons that vary obstacle identity while holding the surrounding spatial configuration fixed. Foundation Models for Robot Planning and Control. Foundation models guide robot policies through different control framework. Policies built on VLM planners let the VLM reason over the scene and instruction, and convert its output into motion through separate planner or controller. Two representative frameworks are code generation, where the VLM writes program that sets planner parameters such as obstacle clearance and speed (Liang et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2023; 2024; Yu et al., 2023), and waypoint selection, where the VLM picks the next waypoint from candidates annotated on the image (Nasiriany et al., 2024b; Fang et al., 2024; Goetting et al., 2025). VLA policies, in contrast, output control actions directly (Kim et al., 2024; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025; NVIDIA et al., 2025b; NVIDIA, 2025; Xiaomi Robotics Team et al., 2026). However, these models ability to adapt their executed motion to different obstacle types remains underexplored.

sections.title: 3 OSMA-BENCH BENCHMARK
sections.content: Built on RoboCasa1 (Nasiriany et al., 2024a), we introduce OSMA-Bench, controlled simulation benchmark for diagnosing obstacle-conditioned safe motion adaptation (OSMA) in household navigation. Through simulation, it enables reproducible, trajectory-level paired comparisons by varying obstacle identity, route geometry, and layout while holding all other task conditionssuch as the placement of other objects and the environment styleconstant. Section 3.1 describes the compositional task design, and Section 3.2 defines the metrics for evaluating OSMA.

Fragile and Robust tiers are distinguished primarily by potential collision consequences: contact with fragile object may cause breakage or spillage and create secondary hazards, whereas contact with robust objects generally has lower consequences. Within each matched comparison, all obstacles are at the same location, and distance is measured surface-to-surface to reduce the influence of obstacle size (Appendix C.3). Two Spatial Axes. To test whether motion adaptation generalizes beyond single spatial configuration, we vary route geometry and kitchen layout. Seven route geometries, such as Fridge CoffeeMachine and Microwave Sink, determine the local spatial relationship among the robot, obstacle, and goal. It includes the required turning requirement and approach direction for given startgoal pair. In contrast, five layout variants , such as One-Wall Small and G-Shaped Large, alter the global arrangement of the scene. Consequently, tasks with the same instruction and route yield geometrically different trajectories and motion requirements, allowing us to assess whether motion adaptation persists beyond single spatial configuration. These controlled variations enrich the benchmark while preserving matched comparisons across OCT. Full route and layout specifications are provided in Appendix B.1.

sections.title: 3.2 EVALUATION METRICS
sections.content: Obstacle-conditioned safe motion adaptation (OSMA) cannot be assessed from navigation outcomes alone; i.e., reaching the goal without collision does not reveal whether robot adjusts its motion to the encountered obstacles. We therefore organize our safety evaluation with task-level and motionlevel safety. For task-level safety, we quantify the proportion of collision-free tasks among successful tasks to measure the task-level safety of the navigation (Section 3.2.1). For motion-level safety, we introduce the Semantic Sensitivity Index (SSI), diagnostic metric that quantifies whether motion adaptation follows the expected relative ordering of caution across obstacle tiers (Section 3.2.2). To characterize how the robot moves relative to an obstacle, we first measure motion features among collision-free successful executions. Additional metrics for task success, navigation efficiency and collision severity are defined in Appendix and reported in Appendix E.

sections.title: 3.2.1 TASK-LEVEL SAFETY METRIC
sections.content: We define Task Success Rate (TSR) as the fraction of tasks in which the robot reaches the goal, and Collision-Free Success Rate (CFSR) as the fraction in which it reaches the goal without any collision. However, since low CFSR alone does not reveal whether the policy frequently fails to reach the goal or reaches it with collisions. We therefore use the ratio CFSR/TSR, as our primary task-level safety metric.

sections.title: 3.2.2 MOTION-LEVEL SAFETY METRIC
sections.content: Proximity-normalized Motion Features. To compare motion across obstacle, we first define features that characterize the robots executed motion. Following prior work emphasizing the joint consideration of motion and obstacle proximity (Fox et al., 1997; Wang et al., 2022), we incorporate both factors into our motion features, as the same motion can have different safety implications at different robotobstacle distances. Figure 2 illustrates this by comparing three trajectories within predefined boundary around the obstacle to focus on nearby motion. Compared with the original trajectory (blue-solid), the orange-dash trajectory passes closer at the same speed, while the green-dashdot trajectory follows the same path at twice the speed near the obstacle. Both trajectories can be less safe than the original, yet speed alone cannot distinguish the orange-dash trajectory from the original, and clearance alone cannot distinguish the green-dashdot trajectory from the original. sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENT RESULTS
sections.content: Our experiments address three research questions (RQs). RQ1 evaluates whether VLMand VLAbased policies exhibit OSMA in their executed trajectories. RQ2 examines where semantic-tomotion grounding weakens in VLM-based policies and whether separating control-value inference from task-execution code generation improves OSMA. RQ3 investigates whether semantic-aware prompting and VLM-as-verifier framework can recover OSMA in VLA policies, and whether the remaining limitation arises from recognizing safety-relevant distinctions or grounding them in action generation.

sections.title: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: We evaluate two families of foundation models: vision-language-action (VLA) and vision-languagemodel (VLM). We instantiate VLMs into robot policies with two frameworks: VoxPoser, codegeneration framework (Huang et al., 2023), and PIVOT, waypoint-selection framework (Nasiriany et al., 2024b). This yields three policy groups: VLA, VoxPoser, and PIVOT. We focus on compact, open-weight models because API-hosted models can raise privacy concerns while large models are often impractical under the on-device resource constraints. Comparisons are restricted within same policy groups (VLA, VoxPoser, PIVOT), which share the same viewpoint and action interfaces. All policies are evaluated in closed loop, using shared low-level base controller within each model family. Details are provided in Appendix D. VLA policies. We evaluate four models finetuned on Robocasa environment: Xiaomi-Robotics-1 (XR-1) (Xiaomi Robotics Team et al., 2026), π0.5-Human300 (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025), open-weight OpenTau variant (π0.5-OpenTau) (Tensor, 2025), and GR00T N1.5 (NVIDIA et al., 2025b; NVIDIA, 2025). They are selected as publicly released checkpoints that support mobilebase control. Appendix D.1 details their training data and how each action space is mapped to the RoboCasa controller. VLM-based policies. We evaluate eight recent VLM models: three Qwen models (Qwen3.6-35BA3B, Qwen3.5-4B, and Qwen3.5-9B) (Bai et al., 2025); two Gemma models (Gemma-4-E4B-it and Gemma-4-12B-it) (Gemma Team, 2026); two Cosmos-Reason models (Cosmos-Reason2-8B and Cosmos-Reason2-32B) (NVIDIA et al., 2025a); and one RoboBrain model (RoboBrain2.5-8BNV) (Tan et al., 2026). To instantiate these VLMs as robot policies, we consider two representative frameworks that translate their outputs into robot control. First, following VoxPoser (Huang et al., 2023), we use code generation: VLM generates task-execution code that constructs spatial planning maps and specifies obstacle-specific clearance and velocity. Second, following PIVOT (Nasiriany et al., 2024b), we use waypoint selection: VLM selects the robots next intermediate destination from candidate points marked on the scene image and iteratively refines its choice. We extend this framework with separate VLM query for speed settings along the path to the selected waypoint. Implementation details for both frameworks are provided in Appendix D.2.1 and D.2.2, respectively.

sections.title: 4.2 RQ1: DO FOUNDATION MODELS GENERATE OBSTACLE-CONDITIONED SAFE MOTION?
sections.content: Figure 3a plots CFSR/TSR against SSI for each policy group. An ideal policy should approach the upper-right corner, which corresponds to collision-free successful on tasks (CFSR/TSR = 100%) and perfect agreement with the expected caution ordering (SSI = 1.0). However, we observe that none of the policies reaches this region. VLAs exhibit low CFSR/TSR and negative SSI. VLA policies show the lowest CFSR/TSR, ranging from 40.6% (π0.5-Human300) to 57.8% (XR-1), indicating that successful executions frequently involve obstacle collisions. To understand why VLM exhibit limited OSMA, we ask whether VLM possesses the safety-relevant semantic knowledge, and if so, why this knowledge fails to translate into control. We conduct our analysis within VoxPoser (Huang et al., 2023), since its generated code allows direct inspection of motion control values. We focus on Qwen3.5-9B, which achieves high CFSR/TSR but an SSI of only 0.384, indicating limited semantic-to-motion grounding. Alongside SSI, we report TSR and CFSR separately rather than their ratio, to assess how the experimental interventions affect task completion and collision-free execution. By examining these control values and their effects on execution, we investigate where the translation from obstacle safety implications to motion breaks down and how it can be improved. The model can assign distinct control values to different obstacles. We first examine whether the model translates obstacle safety implications into numerical control values. In VoxPoser, the model expresses these decisions in generated code through clearance radius RC, velocity v, and its radius RV which defines velocity region where that velocity applies. For example, maintain 50 cm of clearance from the child corresponds to an inferred clearance radius of RC = 50 cm. To assess whether these inferred values follow the expected caution ordering across obstacles, we apply the SSI procedure to control values extracted from the code, yielding value-level SSI as proxy for ordering before execution. Because acceleration and jerk can be obtained from executed trajectories, value-level SSI uses only with the inferred clearance and velocity. As shown in Table 2, Qwen3.5-9B achieves value-level SSI of 0.45, exceeding SSI of 0.38 which is computed from executed trajectories. To determine whether this limited value-level SSI reflects difficulty in inferring obstacle-conditioned control values, we conduct two experiments. (1) Isolated value estimation. We ask the model to infer only control values from the same scene and navigation context, without generating task-execution code (e.g., clearance=35cm, velocity=60% of nominal speed). The model assigns more conservative values to higher-caution tiers, achieving value-level SSI of 0.98. (2) Safety prompt guidance. We augment the original VoxPoser prompts with explicit safety guidance. Although this raises value-level SSI to 0.540.58 and improves SSI by +0.01 to +0.13, the inferred values remain less ordered than under isolated value inference. These findings suggest that jointly generating task-execution code may hinder the models inference of obstacle-appropriate control values. We therefore introduce two-step modular decomposition: task-execution code is generated without numerical values, and the control values are inferred in separate query. This decomposition raises value-level SSI to 0.97, but SSI improves by only +0.01, indicating that appropriately ordered control values do not by themselves ensure OSMA. To understand why improved value-level SSI does not translate into higher SSI, we inspect whether the inferred control values actually take effect during execution. We identify that, for all of these methods, no tasks produce trajectories that enter its assigned velocity region via RV (Vel. = 0% in Table 2). Figure 4(a) illustrates the underlying spatial issue. The inferred control values do not account for the spatial relationship between clearance and the velocity region. Consequently, the planned trajectory does not enter the velocity region, and the assigned speed does not take effect during execution. This interaction shows that the control values cannot be inferred jointly, motivating inference of the velocity-region setting conditioned on the selected clearance. Therefore, we introduce three-step modular decomposition: the model (1) infers RC, (2) infers the target velocity and RV conditioned on RC, and (3) generates task-execution code incorporating these values. This approach improves both SSI and value-level SSI, with the model-inferred velocity-region radius satisfying RV RC + Rbase in 59.0% of tasks. It shows that effective semantic-to-motion grounding requires two conditions: (i) control values that follow the expected caution ordering, and (ii) joint configuration of these values that allows them to affect the executed trajectory.

We investigate this gap between obstacle semantics and action from two complementary angles. First, we examine whether external guidance can reduce collisions and induce OSMA without retraining. Second, we examine VLM backbone within VLA to check whether obstacle safety knowledge remain accessible from the policys own observations. Can External Guidance Reduce Collisions and Induce OSMA? We test two forms of external guidance. (1) Safety prompt guidance varies only the task description. c0 specifies the navigation task alone (e.g., navigate to sink). The conditions are built cumulatively: c1 adds generic obstacle avoidance to c0 (e.g., while avoiding obstacle, the default in Section 4.2), c2 replaces it in c1 with explicit obstacle naming (e.g., avoid the baby), and c3 and c4 each add either caution emphasis (e.g., Be very careful) or behavioral instruction (e.g., slow down and keep distance) to c2. Full prompts are provided in Table 21. (2) Rollout selection samples candidates at each specific interval, and ask external VLM verifier to select the candidate that best satisfies the task and safety requirements. It follows FOREWARN (Wu et al., 2025) except that our verifier observes groundtruth image sequences. We vary the number of sampled rollouts, {4, 8, 16}, and the verifier model, Qwen3.5-9B or Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. We select π0.5-OpenTau for further analysis because it achieves the highest CFSR among the evaluated VLAs while attaining near-best CFSR/TSR (56.7%, compared with the best score of 57.8%). sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduce OSMA-Bench, simulation benchmark that varies obstacle type within matched spatial settings, and the Semantic Sensitivity Index (SSI), which measures whether clearance and proximity-normalized motion follow the expected caution ordering. Current VLMand VLA-based policies do not consistently adapt their motion to obstacle semantics (RQ1). For VLMs, generating control values jointly with task-execution code weakens caution ordering, while separating these processes improves motion adaptation (RQ2). For VLAs, safety prompt guidance and rollout selection yield limited improvements, even though the VLM backbone still partially orders obstacles by caution when queried for control values (RQ3). Together, these results reveal semantic-to-motion grounding gap, highlighting the need for methods that translate obstacle-specific safety requirements into appropriate control parameters and executed motion.

sections.title: A LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK
sections.content: (1) Our study targets navigation in simulation; extending the protocol to manipulation tasks and physical platforms that emulate potentially harmful situations without inducing real-world harm, such as using mixed reality (MR) to augment robot vision, is possible next step. (2) SSI evaluates the ordering of fixed set of motion featuresclearance and proximity-normalized speed, acceleration, and jerkand does not capture other aspects of appropriate behavior, such as approach direction or legibility; human-aligned VLM evaluators could provide more holistic safety assessment. (3) We evaluate compact open-weight VLM-based and VLA policies; adding frontier models as well as classical planners and RL policies would broaden benchmark coverage. (4) The caution tiers define relative ordering of expected motion conservatism within this benchmark, not universal ordering across all contexts; contextand culture-specific variations are beyond the scope of this work. (5) Although obstacles of all tiers share the same position and distances are measured surface-to-surface, obstacle size still affects the available passage width, which may partly confound tier differences in clearance. OSMA-BENCH TASK DETAILS Figure 5 shows the three compositional axes of our benchmark. In addition to the OCT axis introduced in Section 3.1 and illustrated in Figure 5a, route geometry and kitchen layout serve as two spatial axes that vary local and global spatial configurations, respectively, while preserving matched comparisons across OCTs (Figure 5b). B.1 SPATIAL AXES: ROUTE GEOMETRY AND LAYOUT VARIANTS Route geometry. As shown on the left of Figure 5b, we define 7 navigation routes in RoboCasa kitchen environment, each corresponding to different startgoal pair and therefore inducing distinct spatial constraints and interaction patterns: Route (Fridge CoffeeMachine), Route (Fridge Sink), Route (Fridge Stove), Route (Sink CoffeeMachine), Route (Stove MainDoor), Route (Sink Human), and Route (Microwave Sink). These routes induce variations in path length, navigation direction, and turning structure, thereby providing diverse kinematic settings for evaluating motion adaptation. Layout variants. As shown on the right of Figure 5b, we instantiate tasks across five RoboCasabased kitchen layout variants, denoted by layout IDs 04: One-Wall Small, L-Shaped Small, UShaped Small, G-Shaped Small, and G-Shaped Large. We augment the original RoboCasa layouts with safety-related assets and adjust the placement and scale of layout components to support reliable navigation and verification. We exclude the Wraparound and Galley layouts because their narrow geometries leave too little free space for the robot to vary its clearance around the obstacle. We additionally exclude the One-Wall Large, L-Shaped Large, and U-Shaped Large variants because their central island table fully blocks the available routes, forcing identical detour pass regardless of obstacle. This forces the robot to take the same detour across obstacle tiers, making dmin reflect the layout geometry rather than obstacle-conditioned motion adaptation. These variants provide diverse global spatial configurations while maintaining consistent household-kitchen semantics, enabling to evalute motion adaptation under different environmental structures. Additional axis: Style variants. Style therefore offers further axis for evaluating robustness to visual appearance. sections.content: This appendix provides the full definitions and implementation details for the metrics introduced in Section 3.2: an overview of all reported metrics (Section C.2), the notation (Section C.1), the caution tiers (Section C.3), the motion features (Section C.4), the navigation performance metrics and their complementary measures (Section C.5), and the Semantic Sensitivity Index (Section C.6). C.1 NOTATION Table 5 lists the notation used throughout the metric definitions below. The obstacle set = {o1, . . . , oO} includes only safety-relevant obstacles defined by the obstacle caution tier (OCT) and excludes navigation target and source fixtures, so all distance-based metrics measure proximity to obstacles rather than to the goal or start fixtures. Here, oi denotes the i-th obstacle, and di,t denotes the surface-to-surface distance between the robot and oi at time t. Each of the 625 tasks is rolled out once per seed, and we refer to each rollout as task. Time-indexed quantities follow the notation of Section 3.2.2 (e.g., vt, at, jt, and dt). C.2 METRIC OVERVIEW Table 6 summarizes every metric reported in this work, grouped by the aspect of navigation it characterizes; the subsections below give the exact definitions. C.3 CAUTION TIERS We define three caution tiers for obstacle semantics: high-caution living entities, moderate-caution fragile objects, and low-caution robust objects. This hierarchy operationalizes context-dependent caution demand for benchmark evaluation, rather than defining universal safety law or an ISOdefined risk class. Following risk-assessment principles, we regard the caution an obstacle calls for as combination of the severity of the harm collision would cause and the likelihood that collision occurs (ISO, 2010); Table 7 summarizes how the three tiers differ along these two factors.

The same speed is less conservative at smaller clearance: the distance available for stopping shrinks as the robot approaches an obstacle, which is the relationship underlying speed-and-separation monitoring in collaborative robotics (Marvel & Norcross, 2017). The same argument extends to acceleration and jerk for every tier, not only for living entities, around which smooth motion additionally supports comfort and perceived safety (Moller et al., 2021; Singamaneni et al., 2024). Abrupt changes in acceleration are harder for the base controller to track, so the executed path deviates more from the commanded one; close to an obstacle, this deviation consumes larger share of the remaining clearance and raises the likelihood of unintended contact regardless of whether the obstacle is person, vase, or box. What differs across tiers is the consequence of such contact, which is why the ratios are expected to decrease from lowto high-caution obstacles. Mean and maximum features. Mean statistics can smooth over short, abrupt events: brief highjerk swerve or single burst of speed next to the obstacle contributes only small fraction to the mean. The maximum features expose the worst single timestep and thereby reveal whether policy avoids not only sustained aggressive motion but also transient bursts that may be safety-critical near high-caution obstacles. Conversely, because they are intentionally sensitive to single-timestep extremes, maximum features may also reflect transient artifacts or recovery maneuvers rather than consistent tier-dependent caution. We therefore compute both for every task: the SSI of the main text averages over all seven features.

sections.title: D POLICY IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: Common setting The main evaluation comprises 625 tasks, each repeated with environment and policy seeds {0, 3, 16}. Tasks terminate when the environment reports task success (Section C.5) or after 500 control steps. Model Selection. Although OSMA-Bench is model-agnostic and applicable to trajectorygenerating robot-control systems, including classical planners and RL policies, our experiments focus on foundation-model-based policies. Their visual-semantic understanding and language-derived world knowledge make them promising candidates for generating safety-relevant motion adaptations without explicit, entity-specific safety specifications. We prioritize compact, open-weight models as practical baselines for embodied deployment. Most evaluated models contain 4B12B parameters, with the largest containing 35B. Open-weight models avoid reliance on API-hosted services, which can raise privacy and deployment concerns, while substantially larger models are often impractical under the compute and memory constraints of on-device robotic systems. D.1 VLA VLA policies repeatedly generate action sequences from the available observations and execute them before the next policy query. Given natural-language instruction, RGB observations, and the robots proprioceptive state, each policy directly predicts sequence of low-level actions. The controller executes specified number of these actions before the policy receives updated observations and generates the next sequence. Models and checkpoints. We evaluate publicly released checkpoints of XR-1, π0.5-Human300, GR00T N1.5, and π0.5-OpenTau that were trained on RoboCasa demonstrations of the PandaOmron mobile manipulator, rather than the general-purpose base releases, because the benchmark requires policies that produce its 12-dimensional action from its three onboard cameras. Table 11 summarizes their base-model developers, RoboCasa adaptation teams, training data, and adaptation procedures. We keep all policy weights fixed and perform no additional fine-tuning for OSMA-Bench. Because the checkpoints differ in training data and adaptation scope, and their execution settings differ as detailed below, this comparison evaluates the released policies under the stated settings; it does not isolate the effect of model architecture. Input observations. Each policy receives natural-language instruction, RGB images from the robots left, right, and wrist cameras, and proprioceptive measurements comprising the base pose, Images are rendered at the end-effector pose relative to the base, and gripper joint positions. 256 256 resolution. Camera ordering, image preprocessing, state representations, and normalization follow the inference conventions of each released model. Observations are buffered at every control step. At policy query at step t, XR-1 receives observations from steps 6, 4, 2, and t. At 20 Hz, this history spans 0.3 with sampling interval of 0.1 s; each observation contains all three camera views and the robot state. When insufficient history is available, the earliest available observation is repeated. The other policies receive only the current observation. The default instruction is navigate safely to the {dst} while avoiding obstacles, where {dst} denotes the destination. The default VLA inputs do not include top-down images, ground-truth obstacle positions, or caution-tier labels.

As illustrated in Figure 6a, the pipeline follows scene and instruction code generation value maps path planning execution. Given natural-language instruction, top-view RGB observation, and an object-level scene description, the VLM is prompted with fewshot navigation examples to generate Python program π. Executing this program constructs three aligned maps, affordance, avoidance, and rotation, together with velocity setting that assigns speed within region around an obstacle. The generated code explicitly specifies the values used to construct these maps. In Figure 6a, it identifies the coffee machine as the goal, assigns clearance radius of 45 cm to the crawling baby, and sets velocity multiplier of 0.30 within 30 cm of the baby. These instructions construct the affordance map (A), the avoidance map (B), and the region where the assigned velocity is applied (C), respectively. The rotation map, omitted from the illustration, specifies the desired heading. The planner combines the affordance and avoidance maps into cost map and applies search to obtain waypoint path. The rotation map and the assigned velocity provide heading and speed settings along that path, which is executed by the shared waypoint follower described in Section D.2.3. Thus, obstacle-conditioned motion settings are expressed explicitly in generated code, providing the control values examined in our diagnostic analysis. We adapt VoxPoser from 3D manipulation to mobile-base navigation in three ways:

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Value maps are 2D top-down grids over the floor plane rather than 3D voxel grids. The planner uses search on the resulting 2D cost map. Waypoints specify mobile-base poses rather than end-effector targets, with navigation parameters such as obstacle clearance exposed for the generated code to set. What the model actually decides therefore is the control parameters that instantiate each map: for every obstacle, which numerical value enters which map. The affordance map encodes the goal the robot should reach (e.g., move to the coffee machine); the avoidance map encodes the clearance to keep from each obstacle (e.g., stay at least 50 cm from the baby); the velocity setting encodes speed adjustment and the distance within which it is applied (e.g., slow to 60% speed within 30 cm of the baby); and the rotation map encodes the heading along the path. These per-obstacle numbers are the control parameters our analysis inspects. D.2.2 WAYPOINT SELECTION: PIVOT We adapt the iterative visual-prompting procedure of Nasiriany et al. (2024b) to mobile-base navigation and extend it with separate VLM query for speed selection. The pipeline follows observe sample waypoint candidates select and refine waypoints infer speed profile execute. Given an instruction and top-down RGB observation, we overlay 1220 numbered candidate waypoints on the traversable floor. The VLM selects candidates that advance the task while accounting for nearby obstacles. These selections update the proposal distribution, and the candidates are resampled and refined over three rounds to obtain the waypoint for the current navigation leg. Across refinement rounds, candidates are resampled within progressively smaller regions around the VLMs previous selections, allowing it to refine the final waypoint location. Figure 6b illustrates this iterative selection process. The waypoint-selection prompt also includes the motion context of relevant obstacles and their anticipated short-horizon swept regions. This information allows the VLM to consider both current obstacle locations and potential motion when selecting waypoint. The resulting spatial decision is expressed as discrete choice among visually grounded candidates. After selecting , we query the same VLM separately to infer segment-wise speed profile. The segment extends from the robots current position (s = 0) to the selected waypoint (s = 100). The model returns speed multipliers {([sm1, sm], αm)}M m=1, specifying how speed should vary along this segment. The shared waypoint follower executes the navigation leg using the selected waypoint and speed profile, as described in Section D.2.3. The policy then observes the scene again and repeats the procedure. D.2.3 SHARED ACTION OUTPUT AND EXECUTION VoxPoser and PIVOT execute their planned motion through shared holonomic waypoint follower. The follower tracks VoxPosers path or PIVOTs selected waypoints and converts them into lowlevel commands for the PandaOmron robot. Translational commands are scaled by the velocity assigned by VoxPoser, inside the region where it is applied, or by PIVOTs selected speed profile. These commands are executed through robosuites BASIC composite controller. Its 11-dimensional action vector comprises 6-D end-effector pose delta, gripper command, three base velocity commands (forward, lateral, and yaw), and torso command, without control-mode entry. Neither planner directly predicts this vector: the waypoint follower fills the base entries and sets the arm, gripper, and torso entries to zero.

Each condition is evaluated in separate closed-loop rollout, so subsequent observations may differ as the robots actions change. We evaluate five instruction conditions: the task goal alone (c0), add generic obstacle-avoidance guidance (c1, the default in the main evaluation), an explicit obstacle name (c2), an emphasis on caution (c3), and behavioral instruction (c4). Conditions c3 and c4 each add different sentence to c2; the two additions are not combined. Each condition uses the same instruction template across obstacles. None specifies caution tier or tier-specific clearance or speed. Table 21a gives example instructions. We run each condition once on all 625 tasks, with both the environment and policy seeds set to 0, and compare conditions on matched tasks. TSR and CFSR use all 625 tasks. For SSI, we retain only tasks that are collision-free successes under all five instruction conditions c0c4, separately for each model. These subsets support within-model condition comparisons and differ across models. Rollout selection. We augment π0.5-OpenTau with selector inspired by FOREWARN (Wu et al., 2025), using instruction c1 throughout. The selector is invoked every 100 control steps (5 s). At each decision, we save the simulator state and generate candidate rollouts from that state. Each rollout lasts up to 100 control steps, with policy query every 20 steps, and ends early if the task succeeds or the evaluation horizon is reached. Candidates differ only in the initial noise used to generate each action chunk. For each candidate, we render up to six top-down frames at control steps 0, 20, . . . , 100, where step 0 represents the current state. We permute the image order using the verifier seed and decision index; the same index uses the same permutation across tasks. We set the verifier temperature to 0. The verifier receives the task instruction and generic safety condition, without an explicit obstacle name. We evaluate the reconstructed GR00T N1.5 VLM and two Qwen models on the same robot-view inputs from 625 episodes, asking each model to infer control values without generating actions. As shown in Table 26, the reconstructed model achieves value-level SSI of 0.573, with stronger ordering for velocity (τ = 0.794) than for clearance (τ = 0.351). Both Qwen models exhibit more consistent ordering, achieving SSI of 0.978 and 0.990 using clearance and velocity. sections.content: Interpretation and scope. The results indicate that action-head inputs retain information that separately trained classifier can use to distinguish some obstacle types. The 61.7% score belongs to that classifier and does not measure the original action heads recognition accuracy. The experiment also does not measure whether the policy understands obstacle-related risks or uses the available information to avoid contact. The analysis is limited to repeated observations from one model, one route, and three layouts. The feature summaries and classifier settings were chosen during exploratory analysis, and the fixed evaluation subset was formed after the initial analysis. Equal class counts do not equalize task or layout coverage, and training remains uneven across classes. The classifiers may use scene cues associated with obstacle identity in addition to the obstacle itself. The accuracy difference between feature sets does not directly quantify information lost during processing.
